cards.title: Does Nephew resist efficient decision-tree reductions to Lossy-Code?
cards.formal: Prove or refute the source’s concrete conjecture Nephew ≰dt Lossy-Code. In Nephew, given oracle access to two total functions f,g:V→V on an arbitrary finite nonempty set V, output v∈V such that f(f(g(v)))≠f(v) or f(g(v))=v. The relation ≼dt is the deterministic polylogarithmic-complexity reduction defined below; replacing it with randomized or white-box reductions changes the question.
cards.why: Would give a structurally motivated total zero-error randomized search problem beyond the class captured by lossy compression. It tests whether a prominent organizing principle for total search captures Nephew’s finite combinatorial obstruction.
cards.status_note: Primary task definitions, reduction complexity, proven comparisons and the full-version abstract checked with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No Nephew-to-Lossy-Code reduction or nonreduction theorem was located.

progress.text: The source proves Nephew’s TFZPP/PWPP upper bound and several Lossy-Code equivalences, but leaves the Nephew nonreduction conjecture open.

cards.definitions: Encode V by integer labels and encode the two function tables in binary. Let N=|V| and let n denote the total table bit length, Θ(N log(N+1)); the tables are accessed through queries, not supplied for free as readable circuit descriptions. A function-value query can be simulated by O(log(N+1)) bit queries, so either interface gives the same polylogarithmic scale. Lossy-Code_{M→2M} supplies oracle functions e:[M]→[2M] and d:[2M]→[M] and asks for z∈[2M] with e(d(z))≠z. The letters e,d denote expansion and compression; they are unrelated to Nephew’s f,g. For search relations R on n input bits and S on m input bits, an S-formulation of R has a deterministic decision tree F_i computing each target bit i from the source input x, and, for every possible target solution o, a decision tree G_o decoding a source output. It must satisfy (F(x),o)∈S⇒(x,G_o(x))∈R for every x and every valid target solution o. If d_* is the maximum depth of these trees, the reduction’s complexity is log m+d_*. R≼dt S means that this is at most (log(n+2))^{O(1)} for the entire family, with a fixed exponent. The reduction is nonuniform in input length and may describe a target table of quasipolynomial or larger-than-polynomial size as long as log m is polylogarithmic; it cannot inspect that whole table. TFZPPdt consists of total search families with polylogarithmic verification-query complexity and randomized polylogarithmic-depth query algorithms which never return an invalid solution, may return failure, and fail with probability at most 1/3 on each input.
cards.answer_criterion: Show that no family of Lossy-Code formulations of Nephew has complexity bounded by any fixed power of log n; or refute the candidate by giving such a formulation and proving that every target solution decodes correctly. A failure of a particular attempted reduction is not a separation. An efficient reduction would refute the Nephew candidate without settling whether some other natural TFZPPdt problem lies outside LOSSY.

context_blocks.title: Lossy compression must fail somewhere
context_blocks.text: The composition e∘d has at most M possible outputs but there are 2M possible inputs. Consequently at least M strings fail exact reconstruction. cards.title: Are one-clock timed Büchi–Landweber games determined?
cards.formal: Is every game in the source’s one-clock timed model determined: for any finite nonempty move alphabets T,M, any one-clock nondeterministic Büchi timed automaton A over T×M, and either choice of the player who owns L(A), does Timer or Monitor have a winning strategy? The question includes both ordinary one-clock automata and the source’s 1-resetting extension, with the clock semantics specified below. Strategies may use unlimited memory and need not be computable.
cards.why: Would establish whether these timed synthesis models always give one player a mathematically winning strategy, independently of whether that strategy can be computed or implemented with finite memory.

references.title: One-Clock Synthesis Problems
references.authors: Lasota, Sławomir; Lehaut, Mathieu; Parreaux, Julie; Piórkowski, Radosław

cards.definitions: In round i≥1, Timer chooses a_i∈T and a nonnegative rational delay τ_i; after observing this move, Monitor chooses b_i∈M. Put t_i=∑_{j≤i}τ_j. The resulting infinite timed word is ((a_i,b_i),t_i)_{i≥1}. Timestamps may be equal or bounded above: no non-Zeno requirement is imposed. A has finitely many locations, sets of initial and accepting locations, one clock x initially zero, and finitely many transitions (ℓ,(a,b),g,Y,ℓ′), where g is a finite conjunction of x⋈c tests with ⋈∈{<,≤,=,≥,>} and c a nonnegative integer, and Y either resets x to zero or leaves it unchanged. In the ordinary model, delay τ adds τ to the clock before checking g and applying the optional reset. In the 1-resetting extension, the value checked is frac(x+τ), its fractional part; that value is retained unless the transition resets it. A word belongs to L(A) iff some run visits accepting locations infinitely often. Neither player controls this accepting-run existential quantifier. The designated owner wins exactly words in L(A), and the other player wins its complement. A Timer strategy maps finite Monitor histories to the next pair (a,τ); a Monitor strategy maps nonempty histories of Timer’s letters and timestamps to the next b. Each player can reconstruct its own past moves from its strategy. A strategy wins if every opposing response sequence yields a winning word. Determinacy requires the existence of one such strategy; a finite-state controller or synthesis algorithm is an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that at least one player has a winning unrestricted strategy in every game for both specified clock variants, or give a game in one of these variants in which neither player has a winning strategy. Undecidability of deciding the winner, or failure of finite-memory strategies, is not a nondeterminacy example.

context_blocks.title: One player controls time; both choose letters
context_blocks.text: Timer announces a letter and how much time has elapsed. Monitor sees that information before answering. The automaton evaluates their combined infinite timed word. This is a perfect-information turn-based game, rather than a game in which both players simultaneously choose delays.

context_blocks.title: Every play has a winner, but that is not determinacy
context_blocks.text: For any completed play, membership in L(A) decides the winner. Determinacy asks for a stronger statement: before the opponent’s future choices are known, can one player choose a rule that wins against all of them?

context_blocks.title: A simple determined example
context_blocks.text: Let both alphabets be {0,1}, let Monitor own the language of words in which a_i=b_i in every round, and let A ignore its clock. Monitor wins by replying with the observed a_i. General nondeterministic timed winning languages need not have such an immediate response rule.

context_blocks.title: The paper settles synthesis questions, not this existence question
context_blocks.text: The source proves undecidability across its synthesis variants, already with one clock, and studies when a finite controller suffices. It explicitly leaves determinacy unresolved. An undecidable winner problem can still have a winner for every individual game.

context_blocks.title: The clock conventions are part of the question
context_blocks.text: Replacing rational delays by arbitrary real choices, forbidding convergent time sequences, restricting strategies to controllers, or assigning control of nondeterministic runs to a player changes the game. The 1-resetting extension also has its own transition semantics and is included explicitly.

cards.title: Does bounded neighborhood VC dimension suffice for fast geometric diameter tests?
cards.formal: Conjecture 8 asks whether Diameter-Δ for intersection graphs of constant-description-complexity geometric objects always admits a truly subquadratic algorithm when the VC dimension of the radius-Δ neighborhoods is bounded by a constant, in any ambient dimension. The effective object representation, treatment of Δ and allowable parameter dependence still need to be specified for one fully quantified algorithmic statement.
cards.why: Seeks a common structural reason that geometric diameter problems admit faster algorithms. A valid general theorem would turn bounds on reachable-set complexity into algorithmic guarantees across shape families and dimensions.
cards.status_note: Full Conjecture 8, graph model, examples and related framework abstract checked with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No general resolution was located. The universal object-description and parameter conventions remain underspecified.

progress.text: The related framework gives sparse bounded-VC and several specific geometric diameter algorithms.

sentences: The input is a collection of geometric objects whose intersections implicitly form a graph.
The conjecture asks whether bounded VC dimension of radius-Δ neighborhoods always permits a truly subquadratic diameter-threshold test.
Simple neighborhoods may coexist with quadratically many edges, so explicit edge enumeration is unsuitable.
The source proves that the converse is false: some fast cases have unbounded VC dimension.
The general effective object model and dependence on Δ and dimension still need to be fixed.

cards.definitions: Given n geometric objects O₁,…,O_n, their intersection graph has one vertex per object and an undirected edge ij exactly when O_i∩O_j≠∅. The input is the object descriptions, so the potentially quadratic set of edges is implicit. Graph distance dist(u,v) is the number of edges in a shortest path, and is ∞ across components. The diameter is max_{u,v}dist(u,v). Diameter-Δ asks whether it is at most the integer Δ or greater than Δ (equivalently at least Δ+1 for finite distances). Define N^Δ[v]={u:dist(u,v)≤Δ}, including v itself. A subset S of vertices is shattered by these neighborhoods if for every A⊆S there exists v with N^Δ[v]∩S=A. The VC dimension is the largest |S| that can be shattered. A constant bound must hold uniformly over growing inputs in the selected class. Bounded distance VC dimension, using all radii simultaneously, is a stronger condition than the fixed-radius version. Truly subquadratic time means O(n^{2−η}) for some fixed η>0, allowing logarithmic factors to be absorbed into a smaller positive exponent saving. Constant description complexity means a bounded number of defining parameters or predicates per object; without further restrictions it does not specify how those predicates are encoded or evaluated.
cards.answer_criterion: Fix the representation and parameter quantifiers, then prove the universal sufficient-condition algorithm or give a counterexample within that model. The time must be truly subquadratic in the number of objects, with the stated uniform exponent saving. Showing tractability for a new single shape family is progress, but does not establish the general conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Neighborhoods describe who can be reached quickly
context_blocks.text: For a fixed vertex v, N^Δ[v] records all objects reachable from it in at most Δ intersections. Bounded VC dimension says these reachable sets cannot realize every pattern on a large collection of test vertices. It limits their combinatorial variety, rather than their sizes.

context_blocks.title: Even a dense graph can have simple neighborhoods
context_blocks.text: If all objects intersect one another, the graph is complete and every radius-1 neighborhood is the whole vertex set. Its VC dimension is zero, although the graph has Θ(n²) edges. This is why the algorithm must work from object descriptions rather than enumerate all edges.

context_blocks.title: The conjecture is only a sufficient condition
context_blocks.text: The paper gives a subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for boxes despite unbounded relevant VC dimension. Thus unbounded VC dimension does not by itself imply hardness, and an “if and only if” reformulation would contradict a result in the source.

context_blocks.title: Existing bounded-VC algorithms do not cover every implicit graph
context_blocks.text: A related framework has time depending on the edge count m for general sparse graphs, alongside stronger results for specific geometric families. Substituting m=Θ(n²) does not produce the desired O(n^{2−η}) guarantee. The extra geometric input structure remains relevant.

context_blocks.title: Disks provide a concrete unresolved test case
context_blocks.text: The source highlights ordinary disks of varying radii in the plane: their intersection graphs have bounded distance VC dimension, but the paper does not know a truly subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for them. This is distinct from the already solved unit-disk case.

cards.title: Robust regression with Õ(d ε² κ²) samples beyond εκ≈1
cards.formal: For Gaussian covariates with unknown covariance, can a polynomial-time robust-regression estimator use Õ(d ε² κ²) samples when κ≤√d and achieve the source’s intended nontrivial prediction error in the regime εκ≫1? The sample and conditioning bounds are recovered; a precise error benchmark and its signal/noise assumptions still need to be selected from the source’s discussion.
cards.why: Would locate how sample requirements and ill-conditioning interact in computationally efficient robust regression when adversaries can corrupt the entire observation. The distinction between signal-relative and noise-relative error is essential to assessing the claimed advance.
cards.status_note: Published definitions, positive theorem, lower-bound discussion and conclusion checked with the May 2026 record and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching algorithm was located, but the selected question still needs one exact “nontrivial error” guarantee.

progress.text: The COLT paper gives a fast small-εκ estimator and restricted-model evidence for the sample threshold, leaving a matching useful estimator in the larger-product regime open.

sentences: Robust regression must estimate a linear predictor after an adversary corrupts some entire observations.
The proposed sample budget is Õ(d ε² κ²) with condition number κ at most √d.
The target regime has large εκ, beyond the assumption used by the paper’s fast positive algorithm.
Low-degree lower bounds motivate the sample scale but do not establish hardness for every efficient estimator.
The precise meaning of useful error, including signal and noise normalization, remains to be fixed.

cards.definitions: The clean data satisfy X∼N(0,Σ) in ℝ^d and Y=⟨X,β⟩+η, where Σ is positive definite and unknown, β∈ℝ^d is unknown, and η is independent mean-zero noise. Write σ²=Var(η), κ=λ_max(Σ)/λ_min(Σ), and ‖u‖_Σ=√(uᵀΣu). The prediction error of an estimate β̂ is ‖β̂−β‖_Σ; its square is E_X[(⟨X,β̂⟩−⟨X,β⟩)²] on a fresh clean covariate. Strong ε-contamination permits an adversary, after seeing n independent clean pairs, to replace up to εn entire pairs (X_i,Y_i) arbitrarily. Thus both covariates and responses may be corrupted. The zero estimator has error ‖β‖_Σ, so beating zero must be measured relative to this signal strength. The proposed sample scale is n=Õ(d ε² κ²), where Õ suppresses logarithmic factors; κ≤√d implies d ε² κ²≤ε²d². The source’s fast positive theorem uses independent noise with bounded fourth moment O(σ⁴), while its hard instance uses Gaussian noise. A theorem for only Gaussian noise and one for the whole bounded-fourth-moment class have different scopes. The expression εκ≫1 denotes a large-product regime rather than the small-product assumption εκ≲1 in the positive theorem.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify the error, confidence, noise and parameter regime, then give an estimator meeting that guarantee uniformly against strong contamination using the stated samples and polynomial time, or prove an appropriately scoped impossibility. A low-degree or SQ lower bound alone is evidence about particular algorithm classes, not a proof that no polynomial-time estimator exists.

context_blocks.title: The geometry of the error matters
context_blocks.text: If Σ=diag(1,κ), a coefficient error of size one along the first coordinate has prediction norm one, while the same Euclidean error along the second has norm √κ. The Mahalanobis prediction norm captures this difference and cannot be replaced by an unqualified Euclidean error.

context_blocks.title: The recovered sample count has ε in the numerator
context_blocks.text: The target is d·ε²·κ² up to logarithms, not d/(ε²κ²). For fixed small ε and κ=d^{1/4}, it has order ε²d^{3/2}; at κ=√d it reaches ε²d². The motivating gap concerns obtaining useful estimates before that latter scale.

context_blocks.title: Known fast algorithms cover a different product regime
context_blocks.text: The source’s main algorithm uses Õ(d/ε⁴) samples and obtains O(σ√(εκ)) prediction error when εκ is sufficiently small. The selected open question concerns large εκ, where that theorem’s assumptions no longer hold.

context_blocks.title: Restricted-model lower bounds suggest the proposed scale
context_blocks.text: The paper develops a low-degree testing lower bound with threshold Õ(min{d ε² κ², ε²d²}) and an SQ lower bound in a different regime. These motivate an algorithmic target but do not exclude all possible efficient methods.

context_blocks.title: Better than zero needs a quantitative meaning
context_blocks.text: When β=0, the zero estimate already has zero prediction error. More generally its error can be much smaller or larger than σ√(εκ), depending on the signal. A constant-factor improvement over zero therefore cannot be interchanged with a noise-scaled error guarantee without a signal assumption.

cards.title: Does prior entanglement reduce pyramid positional proof systems to PSPACE?
cards.formal: For the source’s pyramid arrangement of verifiers and honest provers, does requiring soundness against malicious provers with arbitrarily much pre-shared entanglement limit the resulting quantum positional proof class to PSPACE? The source asks for this collapse informally; its formal QPMIPˢ definition covers the no-prior-entanglement model, so the modified class and timing conventions still need to be fixed.
cards.why: Would identify whether the quantum advantage in this geometric proof model depends essentially on excluding prior entanglement among adversaries. It separates protocol security under a changed physical resource assumption from an upper bound on the entire resulting complexity class.
cards.status_note: Full open passage, formal separable model and pyramid result checked with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching collapse theorem was located. The proposed entangled-adversary class is not fully specified by the selected passage.

importance.reason: A complexity-class question about the role of prior entanglement in positional quantum proof systems. Existing numerical score retained.

sentences: Positional proofs restrict communication through locations and message-arrival deadlines.
The paper exhibits an arrangement whose classical proofs capture PSPACE while its no-prior-entanglement quantum proofs include EXP.
The open question asks whether allowing malicious provers arbitrary prior entanglement removes that quantum advantage.
Breaking the exhibited protocol alone would not prove the required upper bound for every protocol.
The entangled-adversary variant must still specify its initialization, timing and acceptance conventions.

cards.definitions: A positional proof places verifiers and honest provers at points p(Q) of a metric space (X,d). A message emitted at time t cannot reach another point before its distance-dependent arrival time. In the formal model, time is discrete, d is integer-valued, the timeout and verifier computation are polynomial in the input length, and quantum messages are passed through local completely positive trace-preserving operations. Malicious strategies may change prover locations while keeping verifier locations fixed and must obey the specified routing and timing constraints. A verifier’s min-ball is B_V={z:d(z,p(V))≤min_P d(p(P),p(V))}. The min-ball condition holds when two such balls are disjoint. In the geometric pyramid illustration, k verifiers lie on a regular k-gon of circumradius R in the plane z=0, another verifier lies at height √(4r²−R²) for r>R, and each of k honest provers lies at the midpoint between a polygon verifier and the top verifier. The balls pairwise intersect but have no common point. PSPACE is the class of languages decidable by deterministic polynomial-space machines; EXP allows deterministic time 2^{poly(n)}. The source’s superscript s means separable initial prover resources and its associated no-PE transmission rules. Arbitrary prior entanglement would permit a joint quantum state across malicious prover locations before verifier challenges, with no fixed finite bound on its dimension; this is a change to the soundness model, not a theorem about the original no-PE class.
cards.answer_criterion: Precisely define the entangled-adversary variant and prove that every language with a proof in that class lies in PSPACE, with the claimed lower inclusion if stating equality; or establish a counterexample under explicitly stated complexity assumptions. Demonstrating failure of the source’s particular EXP construction establishes an attack on that protocol, not a collapse of all protocols for the arrangement.

context_blocks.title: Geometry limits who can coordinate before a deadline
context_blocks.text: If a response must arrive quickly, some distant participants cannot exchange the necessary information in time. Positional proof systems use those restrictions while allowing communication whenever the geometry permits it.

context_blocks.title: Pairwise overlap does not give one central location
context_blocks.text: Three disks can overlap in every pair while sharing no common point. The pyramid arrangement creates the analogous difficulty for verifier min-balls: pairwise coordination may be possible even though no single location can answer everyone within the required timing windows.

context_blocks.title: The proved separation uses no prior entanglement
context_blocks.text: For the exhibited arrangement, the source proves that classical positional proofs capture PSPACE, while the separable quantum model contains EXP. This is a conditional separation in computational power unless EXP=PSPACE. It does not establish soundness against pre-entangled malicious provers.

context_blocks.title: A stronger adversary changes which protocols are sound
context_blocks.text: Adding an adversarial resource can invalidate a protocol’s rejection guarantee. The question asks whether that change removes the advantage of all quantum positional protocols for this arrangement. It is distinct from giving honest participants more computational power.

context_blocks.title: The model change is the remaining formalization step
context_blocks.text: The article carefully defines separable initialization, honest and malicious transmission functions, and position-dependent classes. The open entangled variant must say which of these components change before its complexity can be compared with PSPACE.

notes: Recovered the source’s geometry, model and proposed change of adversarial resource.
statement_review.remaining_issue: The open passage proposes allowing malicious provers arbitrary pre-shared entanglement, but continues to use the notation defined only for separable initialization and transmission rules. A complete theorem must fix the modified initialization and pre-input/pre-message communication rules, whether honest provers gain the same resource, the precise growing pyramid arrangement and discrete timing implementation, and the acceptance-gap convention. One must also distinguish collapse of the entire resulting proof class from a cheating attack on the one exhibited EXP protocol. The latter alone would not prove a PSPACE upper bound.

cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability from the connector pattern in monotone CSPs
cards.formal: Let Γ be any fixed finite constraint language on finite ordered domains for which Monotone-CSP(Γ) is NP-hard. If the connector pattern fg-preserves (Γ,Mo), in the explicit monotone-image sense below, must Monotone-CSP(Γ) be fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by its number k of variables? This is the unproved tractability implication of the proceedings’ Conjecture 14; its complementary hardness direction and the binary-relation case are already established there.
cards.why: Would give a structural tractability boundary for constraint systems with few variables and arbitrarily large ordered domains. It extends the known binary case to higher-arity relations, where the same graph-width arguments do not directly apply.
cards.status_note: The full-version algebraic definitions and later proceedings’ exact Conjecture 14 checked, with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No general higher-arity FPT theorem or matching counterexample was located. The source-version difference in connector conventions is recorded explicitly.

cards.definitions: An instance has a finite ordered domain D={1,…,N}, whose size N is encoded in unary; variables x₁,…,x_k ranging over D; and a conjunction of constraints R(m₁(x_{i₁}),…,m_r(x_{i_r})). Here R⊆E^r is a relation from the fixed language Γ, with fixed finite ordered domain E, and each supplied map m_j:D→E is nondecreasing and represented explicitly by its values. Repeated variables in a constraint are allowed. The instance is satisfiable if some assignment in D^k satisfies every constraint. The domain size N is unbounded and is not the parameter. FPT means a deterministic algorithm of time f_Γ(k)·L^{c_Γ}, where L is the entire input length, f_Γ is computable and c_Γ is a constant independent of k,N and the instance. Define the connector pattern by con(0,0,1,2,2)=0 and con(0,2,1,0,2)=1 on the ordered pattern domain {0<1<2}. For each ordered E, form the partial set-valued operation con_E by all nondecreasing maps from that pattern domain into E. Explicitly, for every a≤b≤c in E, include a among the outputs on (a,a,b,c,c), and include b among the outputs on (a,c,b,a,c); no other outputs are included. Empty output means undefined. The pattern fg-preserves (Γ,Mo) when, for each r-ary R∈Γ and any five tuples u¹,…,u⁵∈R, every coordinatewise selection v_j∈con_E(u¹_j,…,u⁵_j) produces v∈R whenever all coordinates have an available output. Equivalently, the Cartesian product of these output sets is a subset of R. This specifies the monotone-image predicate appearing in Conjecture 14; it is not an appeal to an undefined structural “connector property”.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an FPT algorithm for every fixed Γ satisfying the stated premises, with arbitrary fixed relation arities and an exponent independent of k; or refute that implication by establishing a qualifying language whose problem is not FPT. If a negative conclusion relies on FPT≠W[1] or another complexity assumption, state that dependence explicitly. Merely giving an N^{O(k)} algorithm or reproving the binary case does not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Few variables do not make an unbounded domain harmless
context_blocks.text: Brute-force search tests N^k assignments. For any fixed k this is polynomial in N, but its exponent grows with k. FPT asks for one fixed exponent on the input length, moving all unrestricted dependence on k into f_Γ(k).

context_blocks.title: A constraint first coarsens each variable’s value
context_blocks.text: A guarding map may send all values below a threshold to 0 and all remaining values to 1. A fixed Boolean relation then constrains the resulting bits. Different constraints may use different thresholds for the same variable, so a small base language can still describe a rich large-domain instance.

context_blocks.title: What preservation tests
context_blocks.text: For R₃={(0,0),(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(2,2)}, apply the two connector identities to the two columns of these five tuples. The resulting pair is (0,1), which is absent from R₃. Thus R₃ fails the stated preservation predicate. The source uses this relation to describe the hardness side.

context_blocks.title: The remaining step concerns higher arity
context_blocks.text: The proceedings prove an FPT result for binary languages preserved by the connector and establish the complementary W[1]-hardness direction under the stated qualifications. The missing universal tractability claim allows constraints of arity three and higher.

context_blocks.title: The numbered formulation fixes the convention
context_blocks.text: The final prose abbreviates the conjecture as an equivalence. Conjecture 14 supplies its NP-hardness qualification and writes preservation relative to monotone maps. The older full version’s named connector property also includes order-reversing maps. The explicit definition here follows the numbered proceedings statement, so those predicates are not silently conflated.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
